questions.prompt: For a gas that remains in a single gas phase, which conditions generally make the ideal-gas approximation most appropriate?
options: Low pressure and high temperature.
High pressure and low temperature near condensation.
High pressure at any temperature, because crowding makes particle volume negligible.
Low temperature at any pressure, because slow particles cannot attract one another.
questions.explanation: A is correct. Low density makes particle volumes small relative to the available space, and high temperature reduces the importance of attractions relative to particle kinetic energy. B favors both crowding and attraction-related departures. C reverses the finite-volume argument: crowding makes particle size more important. D reverses the attraction argument: slower particles can be more strongly affected by intermolecular attractions. The statement is a general trend within a gas phase, not a claim that every gas is ideal at one universal pressure or temperature.

questions.prompt: A gas has a measured pressure below nRT/V at known n, T, and V. Assume the measurements are accurate and attractive interactions dominate other deviations. Which explanation is consistent with the lower pressure?
options: Attractions force the particles to strike the wall with more momentum than in the ideal model.
Finite particle size always lowers wall-collision rates by increasing the freely available space.
Attractive interactions reduce the wall-directed momentum transfer relative to the noninteracting ideal model.
The ideal equation must predict a lower pressure whenever attractions are present.
questions.explanation: C is correct. Attractions can pull particles back toward the surrounding gas and reduce the momentum transfer responsible for wall pressure compared with the ideal prediction. A predicts the opposite direction of effect. B reverses the finite-volume effect: finite particle size reduces, rather than increases, freely available space. D reverses the comparison: the measured pressure is lower than the ideal prediction under the stated attraction-dominated conditions. Accurate n, T, and V are necessary to interpret the discrepancy in this way.

questions.prompt: At very high density, repulsive finite-volume effects dominate a real gas’s departure from the point-particle model. At the same n, T, and container V, which pressure comparison is expected from that model?
options: The measured pressure must be lower because particle size increases the space available for center-of-mass motion.
The measured pressure can be higher because finite-sized particles have less freely available space than ideal point particles.
The measured pressure must be exactly ideal because container volume alone eliminates size effects.
The measured pressure can only be lower because real gases always have attractions, even when repulsive effects dominate.
questions.explanation: B is correct. Finite particle size and short-range repulsion become important when the sample is crowded; the point-particle approximation overestimates the freely available space. These effects can raise pressure above nRT/V. A reverses the available-space change. C ignores the distinction between geometric container volume and the space available to finite particle centers. D assumes attractions must always determine the sign, ignoring the explicitly dominant repulsive finite-volume effects. The question explicitly states which effect dominates; it does not say every real gas always lies above the ideal pressure.

questions.prompt: Nonpolar gases X and Y have similar particle volumes, but X is much more polarizable. Compare them at the same n, T, and V in a regime where attractions dominate deviations. Which prediction is most consistent with the model?
options: Y must deviate farther below the ideal pressure because weaker attractions always cause larger negative deviations.
Neither can deviate because nonpolar particles have no attractive interactions.
X must lie above ideal pressure because stronger attractions increase available volume.
X can show a larger downward pressure deviation because its more polarizable particles have stronger dispersion attractions.
questions.explanation: D is correct. Greater polarizability can strengthen dispersion interactions even in nonpolar gases. With particle volumes comparable and attractions stated to dominate, X can show a stronger negative departure. A reverses the relation between attraction strength and the stated effect. B ignores dispersion. C gives the wrong pressure direction and misidentifies attraction as a source of extra available volume. Specifying the regime avoids treating polarizability alone as a universal ranking at every density and temperature.

questions.prompt: A gas is heated at fixed n and V in a moderately dilute regime where attraction-related deviations dominate and finite-volume effects are small. Why does increasing temperature generally reduce the relative importance of those deviations?
options: Greater particle kinetic energy makes the attractive interactions less influential relative to the thermal motion.
Heating physically removes every intermolecular force from the gas.
Heating reduces the mole amount even though the container is sealed and no reaction occurs.
Heating makes the particle radii exactly zero.
questions.explanation: A is correct. The attractions do not have to vanish; they become less important relative to the higher thermal kinetic energy. B confuses a reduced relative effect with complete removal of forces. C violates the fixed amount and no-reaction conditions. D turns a useful approximation into a literal disappearance of particle size. The statement concerns the specified dilute attraction-dominated regime, not a universal claim that all volume-related departures vanish on heating.

questions.prompt: A single-phase real gas is expanded isothermally to a much larger volume without losing particles. It becomes very dilute. Which change helps the ideal approximation become more accurate?
options: Every individual molecule becomes physically smaller as the container expands.
Particle volume occupies a smaller fraction of the container and interactions between widely separated particles become less important.
The number of molecules falls in proportion to density, despite the absence of a leak.
The particles stop moving because they encounter one another less often.
questions.explanation: B is correct. Lower density reduces the significance of finite particle size relative to container volume and weakens the influence of interactions between separated particles. A confuses sample dilution with a change of molecular dimensions. C confuses number density with the conserved total number. D confuses collision frequency with the existence of thermal motion. The prompt keeps the sample in a gas phase, so an intervening phase transition is not being used to explain the trend.

questions.prompt: In a hypothetical isothermal compression experiment that remains in a single gas phase, the ratios Pmeasured/(nRT/V) are 0.99 at low density, 0.86 at intermediate density, and 1.20 at very high density. Which interpretation is consistent with these data?
options: Attraction alone must raise the high-density pressure above ideal, so finite particle volume can never matter.
The gas is exactly ideal at all three densities because every ratio is positive.
Attractions can dominate the negative intermediate-density departure, while repulsive finite-volume effects can dominate the positive high-density departure.
Once the ratio is below one it cannot rise above one unless the amount changes, so the observations must reflect a leak.
questions.explanation: C is correct. A ratio below one means measured pressure is lower than the ideal baseline; a ratio above one means it is higher. Opposing attraction and finite-volume/repulsive effects can produce the observed change in sign. A assigns the positive high-density effect to attractions alone. B confuses a positive ratio with the ideal value of one. D imposes an unjustified monotonic rule and assigns a leak without evidence; competing effects can change the sign at fixed amount. These data are a hypothetical model comparison, not measurements copied from a particular gas.

questions.prompt: A real-gas sample gives PV/(nRT) very close to one at one measured condition. What conclusion is justified?
options: The ideal equation is accurate at that condition within measurement precision, but this does not prove attractions and finite-volume effects are individually zero.
The particles must literally have zero radius.
The sample must obey the ideal equation exactly at every other pressure and temperature.
All intermolecular attractions must be absent, regardless of possible volume effects.
questions.explanation: A is correct. A small net departure can result from individually small effects or from partial cancellation of opposing effects. Agreement at one condition does not establish the literal ideal assumptions or all-condition behavior. B turns an approximation into proof of zero particle size. C extrapolates one observation to every condition. D rules out attractions without separating their contribution from finite-volume effects. Measurement precision also limits what a near-unity ratio can establish.

questions.prompt: A rigid insert occupies part of a vessel. A student uses the empty vessel’s larger volume to calculate nRT/V, but the gas can occupy only the space outside the insert. The measured pressure is higher than that calculation. What should be done before attributing the difference to gas nonideality?
options: Conclude immediately that the gas molecules are large, because every high pressure proves finite-volume effects.
Conclude that attractions increased the pressure, without checking the volume.
Ignore the insert because ideal point particles can occupy the solid insert’s interior.
Use the actual accessible gas volume; the incorrect larger volume can itself make the predicted pressure too low.
questions.explanation: D is correct. Even an ideal gas in the smaller accessible volume has a pressure greater than a calculation using the empty vessel’s larger volume. A confuses a possible measurement/model-input error with proof of molecular excluded-volume effects. B gives attractions the wrong typical pressure effect and ignores the known error. C confuses negligible molecular size with the ability to pass through a macroscopic solid. Reliable n, T, V, and pressure calibration are needed before interpreting a discrepancy as intrinsic nonideality.

questions.prompt: Two gas samples at the same temperature and container volume have different measured pressures, but their mole amounts are unknown. A student concludes that the higher-pressure sample must deviate more from ideal behavior. Which evaluation is best?
options: The conclusion follows because larger absolute pressure always means a larger measured-minus-ideal difference.
The conclusion is unsupported without an ideal baseline for each sample, which requires the mole amounts as well as T and V.
The conclusion can be checked from the elements’ proton numbers alone.
Only molar mass is needed to predict each pressure, regardless of the amount present.
questions.explanation: B is correct. Pressure magnitude is not itself a deviation: each sample must be compared with its own nRT/V baseline. More moles can give a higher pressure even for perfectly ideal gases. A equates an absolute measurement with its difference from an unknown baseline. C substitutes nuclear identity for the missing amount and molecular-interaction information. D omits amount; molar mass alone does not determine n without a corresponding mass measurement. This distinction is necessary for a controlled comparison of real-gas behavior.

questions.prompt: A known mass of gas has a pressure below its ideal value because attractions dominate; finite-volume effects are negligible. A student estimates its molar mass using M = mRT/(PV) with the measured P, V, and T. How does the estimate compare with the true molar mass?
options: It is too small because the measured pressure is too small.
It is exactly correct because molar mass is an intrinsic property, regardless of the model used to calculate it.
The direction cannot be determined unless the proton count is known.
It is too large because a smaller measured pressure appears in the denominator.
questions.explanation: D is correct. Let Pmeasured = r(nRT/V), with r < 1. The ideal-based calculation gives Mcalculated = mRT/(PmeasuredV) = (m/n)/r = Mtrue/r, which is too large. A reverses the denominator effect. B confuses a fixed true property with an estimate obtained using an inaccurate gas model. C introduces an unnecessary variable; the stated pressure-departure direction is enough. If a different effect made the pressure greater than ideal, the error direction could reverse, which is why the attraction-dominated condition matters.
